2.21 Fauna. By providing most of the water in this arid region, the Rio Grande is a valuable resting area for many migrant bird species as well as a permanent home for numerous species of wildlife. Brush covered rocky slopes and dense thickets along the river provide food and cover for a variety of small animals. Insects and rodents are the most numerous inhabitants of the grassy openings amid the rocks and brush. Species of rodents in the area reported by the National Park Service (USDI, 1976) and Davis (1974) include the fox squirrel, rock squirrel, 3 ground squirrels, 3 gophers, 12 mice, 6 rats, muskrat, porcupine, and nutria. Hares and rabbits include the California jack rabbit, eastern and audubon cottontails (Davis, 1974). Cloven-hoofed mammals in the area are javelina, mule deer, and white tailed deer (USDI, 1976). Furbearers in the area are bobcat, raccoon, coyote, skunks, ringtail, gray fox, desert fox, and beaver. Amphibian and reptile species found in the area include 12 frogs and toads, 6 turtles, 1 gecko, 13 lizards, 2 skinks, and 26 nonpoisonous snakes. Poisonous snakes include the blacktailed rattlesnake, western diamondback rattlesnake, banded rock rattlesnake, trans pecos copperhead, broad banded copperhead, cottonmouth, and coral snake (USDI, 1976; USDI, 1974; Raun and Gehlbach, 1972). A variety of ducks and geese pass through the area during migrations and owls, hawks, falcons, and vultures are common residents. Bird species sighted along the river include mourning dove, cardinal, killdeer, great blue heron, roadrunner, and scissor-tailed flycatcher. Colonies of cliff and bank swallows are evident in large concentrations.
2.22 Rio Grande Fishery. The fishery composition of the Rio Grande is similar to that of Lake Amistad with nongame species predominating. Exotic fish species have not been stocked in the river, but walleye fry and fingerlings and Florida bass and striped bass fingerlings have been stocked in Falcon Reservoir. The streambed of the river is generally composed of shifting sand and gravel with very little aquatic vegetation in the river. To protect the exotic species that have been stocked, both the US and Mexican governments have agreed to make all efforts to control illegal netting. At present, no legalized commercial netting occurs on Amistad or the Rio Grande to Falcon.
2.23 The estuarine area of influence generally includes lower Laguna Madre and tidal reaches of the Rio Grande. Also included are the North Floodway and Arroyo Colorado, bypass systems that carry floodwaters of the Rio Grande into the lower Laguna Madre. In addition to flood flows, these drainageways carry local runoff and irrigation return flows to the estuary. Lower Laguna Madre and the tidal reaches of the Rio Grande provide excellent habitat for a variety of marine organisms. Although water quality is often poor, mainly from pesticide runoff from irrigated croplands, the area is an excellent nursery ground for white and brown shrimp, spotted seatrout, and blue crabs. Additional species in the estuarine habitat include black and red drums, flounder, pompano, sea catfish, stripped mullet, menhaden, Atlantic crocker, and oyster. Important forage fishes in the area are pinfish, silver perch, pigfish, and silversides (USDI, 1974).
2.24 Endangered Species. This category covers both plant and animal species, but the fish are of primary concern. Several wildlife species that are considered migrants because their range includes broad habitat types found in the Rio Grande Plains include the mountain lion, oceiot. jaguarundi, and Mexican beaver. Other endangered species possibilities are birds having a statewide range such as the golden eagle, bald eagle, osprey, peregrine falcon, prairie falcon, and merlin.
